maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION TO STUDY STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to inform the house that the government has decided to establish a royal commission on the status of women. The chairman of the commission will be Mrs. John Bird. Other members of the commission will be announced when their appointments have been completed, which I hope will be over the week end.
The royal commission will be asked to inquire into and report on the status of women in Canada and to recommend what steps might be taken by the federal government to ensure their equality with men in all aspects of Canadian society. Its findings will, of course, have to take into account the division of legislative powers between the federal and provincial governments under the constitution.
The commissioners will be free to look into such matters as they feel are relevant, and in particular the following areas:	Laws and
practices under federal jurisdiction concerning the political rights of women; the present and potential role of women in the Canadian labour force, including the special problems of married women in employment and measures that might be taken under federal jurisdiction to help in meeting them; measures that rftight be taken under federal jurisdiction to permit the better use of the skills and education of women, including the special retraining requirements of married women who wish to re-enter professional or skilled employment; federal labour laws and regulations in their application to women; laws,
practices and policies concerning the employment and promotion of women in the federal civil service, by federal crown corporations and by federal agencies; federal taxation pertaining to women; marriage and divorce; the position of women under the criminal law; and immigration and citizenship laws, policies and practices with respect to women.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION TO STUDY STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the right hon. Prime Minister on this announcement. I am extremely sorry that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) is unavoidably absent today; I am sure she would have liked to offer her congratulations, because this is a subject which she has been pursuing for some time.
I think the government's decision to appoint this commission is most commendable. I am very glad to see that the influence of the Secretary of State has prevailed upon her male colleagues to take this very progressive step. We have not had an opportunity to examine the commission's terms of reference, but judging from the remarks the Prime Minister made they seemed to be fairly comprehensive.
I hope the terms of reference will spell out in particular the problems of working women and working mothers; the whole problem of nursery schools; the problem of women who have to hire baby sitters and housekeepers, and the enactment of laws enabling them to charge this as an income tax deduction. There are a great many problems in our modern society which women have to face today which were not common 10 or 20 years ago. I hope the terms of reference will be wide enough to allow a full investigation into the problems which confront modern working women in order that they may have fair treatment, equal to that of men in our society.
May I say to the Prime Minister that the selection of the personnel of this commission is extremely important, and I hope the government will keep in mind not only the professional women and the business executives but also membership on that commission of women who understand the point of view of women in the labour force and the particular problems which confront them at this time.

I am sure nothing but good can come from the investigation the Prime Minister has announced. I hope it will result in some legislation being presented to the house which will help to give women a status equal to that of men in our society.

maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION TO STUDY STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it a very pleasant task indeed to comment on the announcement the Prime Minister just made. I want to make my remarks very brief, but I do not wish to let the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam have the credit for being the only member on this side of the house interested in the rights of women.
I believe the announcement made by the Prime Minister will be welcomed not only by the women of Canada but by all Canadians, because I think it covers an area which has been neglected so far, namely the task of ensuring that the rights of mothers and of working women in this country are equitable in every respect.
I wish to say to the Prime Minister that I believe it is particularly necessary that this commission investigate both the federal and provincial laws to make sure they are applicable equally to men and women; and this applies also to the taxation laws which the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has already mentioned. I will just add that I think it is a good thing this action has been taken, and I believe nothing but good can come out of it. I commend the Prime Minister for making this decision.

the second reading of Bill No. C-261, to establish the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned when moving the resolution preceding this bill, events have made it desirable to move more quickly than was originally intended. The government now feels that it is most desirable to proceed with this legislation at once and, after approval, to proclaim the Canada Deposit Insurance Act with the least possible delay.
It would be undesirable for federal institutions to be insured earlier than insurance would be available to provincial institutions. To expedite making insurance available to provincial institutions it is contemplated that the deposit insurance corporation would be prepared to cover all the existing deposit accepting trust and loan companies of a province if the province concerned so requested, even before the corporation has made an examination into the affairs of the individual companies and ascertained if they were eligible for insurance.
The provinces will be expected in return to enter into appropriate financial arrangements to ensure that any losses which occur as a result of the deposit insurance scheme having become effective prior to inspection will not become the obligation of those institutions which are in a sound position and are contributing to the deposit insurance fund. This would simply be a recognition by the provinces of their responsibility for provincially incorporated institutions prior to the applicability of federal deposit insurance.
It is not our intention in any event, Mr. Speaker, to insist on uniform national standards as a prerequisite to entry into the insurance plan, but to work toward higher minimum standards over a reasonable period of time with institutions which have the desire and capacity to improve their financial standing.
Canada Deposit Insurance Corp.
I realize that by going ahead at once on this proposal we will not have as full consultation with the provinces before the legislation comes into effect as we had originally hoped to have. It is not intended that passage of the legislation will close the door to further discussion with the provinces, and I will continue to give serious consideration to any suggestions that may be made. However, in the light of the views that have been expressed in the house and in the committee which is considering the bank bills, the government has reached the conclusion that we should not delay the availability of deposit insurance while further discussions with the provinces proceed.
There are three major objectives for the proposed system of deposit insurance. The primary objective, of course, is to ensure the safety of the deposits of small investors who are usually not in a position to judge for themselves the financial soundness of the constitutions to which they entrust their savings.
Second, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will also have power to function as a lender of last resort for deposit accepting institutions, providing needed liquidity at times of crisis when such institutions may not have access to their normal sources of liquidity.
Third, member institutions will be subject to inspection. It will be an objective to bring about a gradual improvement in the minimum financial standards of deposit acceptance institutions across the country. There will be a genuinely sympathetic and helpful attitude toward institutions which wish to cooperate in this objective.
Membership in the deposit insurance plan will be obligatory for chartered banks, Quebec savings banks and those federal trust and loan companies which accept deposits from the public. Provincially incorporated trust and loan companies which accept deposits from the public will be eligible to apply for membership if they have the consent of the province concerned.
It is not proposed that deposit insurance be available to credit unions and Caisses Popu-laires, which are co-operative institutions dealing with their members rather than public deposit accepting institutions. To a considerable extent mutual insurance schemes have already been established for the local credit unions. At the federal level there is the Cooperative Credit Associations Act, which provides for the incorporation by special act of the parliament of Canada of co-operative credit societies.
12622	COMMONS
Canada Deposit Insurance Corp.
Amendments to the Co-operative Credit Associations Act are presently under consideration. Among the matters that will be reviewed is whether a lender o i last resort facility is needed in connection with the operation of these societies. As I have already mentioned in the house, I have asked my departmental officials to look at the more general questions surrounding the adequacy of the control that now exists in the field of finance companies, and I have indicated that we are willing to confer with the provinces on this matter if they so wish.
Except in the matter of the maximum size of deposit to be insured, namely $20,000, it has been thought best to leave some room for flexibility in the definition of insurable deposits. It is proposed, therefore, to define the kinds of deposits eligible for insurance under the by-laws of the corporation which will require the approval of the governor in council. All the usual kinds of savings and current deposit accounts will be insured. In addition, it is the intention to include special forms of term and notice deposits and deposit-like instruments which are issued by some institutions.
It may be desirable to ensure a clear, public understanding of what is insured and what is not insured by bringing about some clarification in the names used to describe certain deposit instruments. But so far as the existing situation is concerned, the intention is to go as far as possible to make insurance available for all types of deposits and deposit-like instruments provided only that they are not instruments clearly in the category of securities rather than deposits.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
It is expected that the greatest need for the lender of last resort function of the deposit insurance corporation is likely to arise in relation to the demand or quite short term deposits of insured institutions. To the extent to which the liabilities of financial institutions are of a long term character, given good management they should be able to protect themselves by holding an appropriate distribution of assets. However, in the case of institutions with very short term liabilities, it is difficult for them both to make any profit on their operations and to keep enough short term assets to protect themselves against all emergencies. Even if they maintain high standards of financial management, events taking place elsewhere in the financial system, perhaps

DEBATES	February 3, 1967
outside Canada, can have repercussions that produce serious liquidity problems for them.
Turning now to specific measures involved in the proposal to establish the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, I shall just mention the major features.
First, it is proposed to establish a new crown corporation to be called the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. It will be under the management of a board of five directors, including a chairman of proven financial experience from outside the public service to be appointed by governor in council. The other four directors will be the governor of the Bank of Canada, the deputy minister of finance, the superintendent of insurance and the inspector general of banks.
Second, parliament is asked to provide the $10 million share capital of the corporation, and a deposit insurance fund will be built up out of premiums of one thirtieth of one per cent per annum on the insured deposits of member institutions. When the fund has reached adequate proportions it is provided that the rate of premiums may be reduced under certain circumstances.
Third, the corporation will invest its share capital and the deposit insurance fund in securities of the government of Canada. Earnings on these investments will be available to meet operating expenses and, if there is sufficient net income, to pay dividends on its share capital.
Fourth, to enable the corporation to act as lender of last resort to its members in case of need, either by lending on the security of members' assets or purchasing such assets when that is appropriate, the government will be authorized to make advances to the corporation up to a total of $500 million. Any such advances would be expected to be repaid by the corporation from recoveries of the assistance provided to its members or from the deposit insurance fund.

Mr. Speaker, several days ago we had a relatively short debate at the resolution stage of this legislative measure which concluded with a lot of pushing and prodding of the government by the opposition. The government had not made up its mind, as it indicates it has now, that this bill should be brought on at this stage and referred to a committee. As a matter of fact the original idea was that following the resolution stage the bill would be introduced so the people concerned and the public would have an opportunity to study
February 3, 1967

Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. insurance was established in conditions of extreme crisis in the banking and financial system as a whole. There can be no doubt that in this situation the system helped restore a public confidence that had been buffeted and was confused. That system was also designed to provide a longer run answer to the problems of successive bank failures and of the destructive runs on banks that had afflicted the decentralized unit-banking system of the United States for most of its previous history.
Again, Mr. Speaker, I would point out that there is a difference between the United States and its decentralized unit system of banking and Canada's more centralized and concentrated branch banking system. The Americans had to bring some degree of uniformity to different classes of banks, some of them members of the federal reserve system but most of them non-member banks. An examination of the United States experience will reveal that the crucial element in the operation of the insurance system over the past three decades has been the effective enforcement of standard supervision and inspection over the thousands of deposit taking institutions of all types and sizes that operate in that country.
In Canada no one can assert with any justification that the federally supervised institutions are under a deficient system of supervision. Rather it is those institutions which have been provincially incorporated and operate in a vacuum. I can say nothing better for them than that they operate in a vacuum, because the standards of supervision vary so much.
Under those circumstances, in the government's desire to provide for insurance I find it somewhat strange, as I did at the resolution stage, that there should be an insistence that it be mandatory that the federally supervised institutions shall have deposit insurance. There is no question about it in the bill. But in respect of those who require the insurance, those whose supervision it is essential be upgraded, their participation will be voluntary; and worst of all-and this is where this bill is absolutely incomprehensible-it shall be with the consent of the province that incorporated the institution. This to me is a negation of the constitutional obligation of the government of Canada to have exclusive jurisdiction over banking, currency and interest.
All I can say is that the government is endeavouring to buy some political peace at the expense of enshrining in a statute in the most permanent form some theory of the


right of a province to have a say with regard to banking. This provision is in the bill -"with the consent of the province". In the matter of banking, currency and interest it is clear in the constitution that the exclusive jurisdiction lies with the government of Canada. It is up to those who assert the contrary to show that this jurisdiction is not exclusive. They must assert their own jurisdiction, because jurisdiction in banking cannot exist in a vacuum. Therefore I cannot see why this feature has been introduced into the bill.
Yesterday during discussion in the committee the minister expressed the opinion that it was difficult to define the business of banking. But in this particular bill we have bumped up against much the same sort of thing. We will have the problem of deciding which are deposit taking institutions. There are many ways of defining banking without inhibiting the growth and evolution of that system, and I hope on the appropriate occasion to put forward such a definition.
We will have the problem of defining a deposit taking institution. Why it could not have been assumed in the Bank Act is something about which one must speculate. The bill proposes that this insurance shall be at a flat rate, and therefore denies one of the fundamental principles of insurance; there is no question of risk being a determinant of the rate of insurance.
[DOT] (12:10 p.m.)
Therefore I can flatly state that I think our chartered banks and the major near banks will be made to serve as the milk cows for this scheme. For some of the banks this may mean an expenditure of about $4.5 to $5 million a year. Who will pay for that? It can be said that they have customers and that this charge will be passed on. I do not think one can legitimately insist that the banks should assume this charge. The service is being provided to the customers; therefore it is they who should assume the charge.
In so far as the small institutions are concerned, the requirement that a minimum of $500 or one thirtieth of one per cent of a deposit within a limit of $20,000 per account be assessed each member institution-and it is not per depositor but per account-means that this institution will have to have minimum deposits of $1.5 million or the rate of one thirtieth of one per cent will not be applicable.

During the resolution stage I made representations to the effect that those institutions wishing to become insured members of the corporation should be given the privilege of working up to the required standing. In other words, if they met the minimum standards now they should be allowed to apply and be granted interim certificates, which are of course renewable each year, until they reached the required standing. From the remarks made by the minister I am not too sure whether the Trust Companies Act or the Loan Companies Act will apply to the standard of investment which will be required of these institutions, and what degree of liquidity will be sought.
When the minister makes his statement at the completion of the debate I hope he will give us a much fuller explanation with regard to his statement that all the institutions would be accepted into the scheme if the provincial governments asked for it. There is some confusion in my mind regarding this matter, but let me say that it may be in my mind only and not in the minister's statement. In any event I hope to be given a clearer picture of the interim steps, because I think they are very important. It will be interesting, when this bill is considered in the committee, to get some idea of the regulations which are envisaged; because the bill only marks out the four corners of this scheme, and as a matter of fact a good deal of the law will be embodied in the regulations.
I should like to reiterate the plea I have made on many occasions, that these regulations should be subject to review by this house and by a standing committee of the house, because this corporation is a classic example of delegated powers. It will have very extensive powers, and they must be subject to review by parliament. It is not good enough to say that the regulations are made by order in council and tabled and that hon. members can go and find them. No means is given whereby these regulations may be examined. I urge the minister to assist the house to amend our rules to provide for a standing committee on delegated legislation, so that hon. members may be given a chance to see what is being done and examine it themselves.
The last point I should like to make, and which I should like clarified by the minister either now or in the committee when the bill is sent there, concerns the powers of the deposit corporation. I should like to know whether the corporation will have the right of
Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. sale or merger of an institution which has not been able to meet its obligations.
The power of sale or merger is not specifically dealt with in clauses 11 or 3(1) of the bill. It is said in clause 3(1):
There is hereby established a corporation, to be known as the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, having power to acquire, hold and alienate real and personal property.
I doubt that the wording of this clause is sufficiently wide. I apologize for making specific reference to a clause in the bill; however, I did want to state that this bill should provide for power to be given to the corporation to dispose of the assets of a defaulting institution. It is said in clause 11(c) that the corporation may act as a liquidator. Nevertheless I think it should have the power of sale and of merger.
There are a number of other remarks which could be made with regard to this government proposal, but in view of the remarks which have already been made both by myself and by my colleagues, our main concern now is to see this bill goes to the committee as soon as possible. I will say at this time that we in this party are prepared, with some reluctance, to support this bill on second reading. At this time and under the circumstances the principle of deposit insurance is only second best.
We think the provision with regard to the lender of last resort is good. We have some very serious reservations about the provincial rights which are being established in this regard. As a matter of fact if it were not for some other good features of the bill I would be opposed to it because of that provision. However, in the light of all the circumstances we are prepared to support the bill on second reading.

The members of the New Democratic Party support the principle of deposit insurance and are prepared to facilitate the speedy passage of this bill. The hon. member for Greenwood set forth our support during the debate on the resolution. We look upon our large financial institutions as forming part of the whole of our financial system, and deem it necessary that they be under federal direction, supervision and control. These financial institutions include banks, trust and loan companies, finance companies, credit unions and caisses populaires.
The recent display of waffling in determining jurisdiction, authority and responsibility by the federal government and the government of Ontario with regard to Prudential Finance indicates the necessity for the direct assertion of authority over the financial institutions of our country. We appreciate the jurisdictional problems involved, but we place the security and safety of Canadian depositors and investors in priority to petty jurisdictional problems.
The principle of deposit insurance is twofold; first, to assure the safety of deposits and, second, the supervision and control of our financial institutions. I would prefer to place the second purpose first because the safety of deposits is almost entirely dependent on supervision, inspection and control. I noted an article in the Globe and Mail of Monday, January 30 in which Fraser Robertson reports a statement to the shareholders of Guaranty Trust Company at a recent annual meeting. The president, J. Wilson Berry, pointed with pride to the record of Canadian trust companies, noting that the record of no casualties in the industry has been maintained during a severe time of testing in the past year. He also said that the essential purpose of deposit insurance is the protection of depositors. Mr. Berry then indicated that he did not believe deposit insurance would be of any value to customers of some large, well established trust and loan companies or even the chartered banks.


Surely, Mr. Speaker, the objective of deposit insurance is to prevent losses, not protect against them. What may be safe today in a bank, trust or loan company may be insecure tomorrow. Prevention comes before, and as a necessary and vital step to protection. Mr. Robertson pointed out in his article:
There is no guarantee that I know of that the
management of any company will not deteriorate, that control will not change hands, that the nature of the business will not alter. Governments may force such changes, for instance, by requiring banks to divest themselves of substantial interests in trust companies or by limiting the availability of directors. Again, governments may themselves bring about a change in the nature of a business, as by permitting banks to enter substantially into the mortgage business and to issue debentures, while trust companies are asking for permission to make consumer and personal loans.
The activities of financial institutions in Canada have changed remarkably in recent years in response to the requirements of a vastly changed economy. Thus much of the experience of an old established company will be no greater than that of a relatively young one, and the temptation to believe it cannot err may be a very real danger to the institution and to the public.
There are a few criticisms, Mr. Speaker, which I hope are constructive and which we would like to present to the minister. First, the legislation indicates an almost tacit approval of provincial jurisdiction in the monetary and financial affairs of our country. The provision in the bill which requires consent both by the applicant company and the province with regard to provincial trust and loan companies should not prevail. The voluntary aspect is lost by requiring the consent of the province. The province should require companies to participate in deposit insurance, and should make it a requirement of their licence to do business in the province.
We were very much encouraged by the statement of the premier of British Columbia to the effect that he would compel such companies to take out this insurance as a requirement of doing business in the province. Other provinces should follow this lead. When one knows that most of the large trust and loan companies are provincially incorporated, it indicates the necessity of full participation by all these financial institutions in deposit insurance.
The second criticism we have is that the term "deposit" is not defined in the bill but is left to the governor general in council to determine. We appreciate the difficulties in defining the term "deposit", as to whether it is a deposit or an investment with the institution involved. I note that in the United States the Federal Savings and Loans Insurance
February 3, 1967	COMMONS
Corporation insures the accounts of all forms of savings in insured savings and loan associations, including share and investment certificates, while the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation insures demand savings and time deposits in commercial and mutual savings institutions. This would be a good starting point, Mr. Speaker, toward defining the word "deposit".
I would ask also that all financial institutions be required to notify depositors as to whether the "deposits" were deposits covered by the deposit insurance scheme or were just investments in the shares of the company. This problem was underlined by the recent Prudential fiasco, when people rightly thought deposits in the form of guaranteed investment certificates were the same as cash deposits in our chartered banks. We in the New Democratic Party feel that in those circumstances some form of compensation should be given to those people who invested their money in Prudential. When you have people who are not aware of the difference between a deposit and an investment, the onus is on the financial institution not only to make them aware of it but to compensate them if losses occur.
The third point, Mr. Speaker, is with regard to coverage. We of the New Democratic Party would like to see coverage not only of chartered banks, federal loan and trust companies, but also of provincial trust and loan companies and finance companies. We appreciate the insurance protection that people have with regard to credit unions and the Caisses Populaires. The attraction of the lender of last resort provision in the bill would act as an encouragement and attraction to companies which would otherwise be reluctant to enter into a scheme of deposit insurance. In so permitting these companies to enter the field, we feel some standard should be adopted. Again, I point out information received with regard to deposit insurance in the United States. Before insuring any bank the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation considers the following factors: (1) the financial history and condition of the bank; (2) the adequacy of its capital structure; (3) its future earnings prospects; (4) the general character of its management; (5) the convenience and needs of the community to be served by the bank; (6) the [DOT]consistency of its corporate powers with the purposes of the Federal Deposit Insurance Act. These factors should be given full consideration when companies are making application for deposit insurance.

There is adequate control over banks and federally incorporated trust companies. No one would question their stability and integrity. But large segments of the system, many trust companies, finance and loan companies, operate completely outside the sphere of that federal inspection and control, many such companies not being federally incorporated. Yet these institutions carry on many of the aspects of banking business. The failure to accept the Porter commission recommendation is the first serious omission in the legislative program the government has presented to us in this field. The program almost completely rejects the Porter commission recommendations.

Though this may be traditional, I think it is incredible, indeed inconceivable, that it should be allowed to continue. Mr. Speaker, this bill, I believe, is a vivid illustration of the unique propensity of the government for doing everything backwards, of its affinity for half measures and compromise and of its incredible aptitude for vacillation and irresolution. The bill is compulsory for those who need it least. It is voluntary as well as dependent upon the provinces and least effective for those who need it most. It will protect the public where the least protection is needed. It may well leave the public exposed and imperilled where protection is imperative.
Sir, the basic weakness of the government's approach was stated precisely in another context in the report of the Porter royal commission at page 363:
An alternative, therefore, would be to make the federal regulation voluntary while offering inducements to institutions to submit themselves. Unfortunately, however, those few institutions which are now clearly unregulated are precisely the ones which are likely to remain outside the regulatory framework.
This, sir, is what is likely to happen as a result of this legislation. Those provinces which may need it most are the ones which will not make it imperative upon the institutions within their jurisdiction. But what I find most objectionable in the bill is its admission, both by explicit provision and by inference, that the provinces have a role in the field of banking. This I dispute vigorously and it will be the theme of what I want to say this afternoon, for I object to the abdication and surrender of jurisdiction of this parliament.
I do not believe that the provinces want to intrude in the field of banking. The failure of this parliament in the past to occupy fully the field of banking has enabled the provinces to purport to confer on provincially incorporated institutions of the type now colloquially known as near banks, powers in the field of banking. Do the provinces really want to retain that usurpation of authority achieved by default? I think not.
As an example, sir, I point to an exchange which occurred in the legislature of Ontario as recently as January 26 of this year. At page 25 of the Ontario Hansard the following appears during a speech by Hon. H. Leslie

Rowntree, Minister of Financial and Commercial Affairs of Ontario, dealing with the question of deposit insurance:
-it is the intention of this government to introduce legislation to cover the entire field and to occupy that position in the jurisdictional aspect or nature of the British North America Act which has been abdicated by the federal government.
Our intention is to see that legislation is made available by this government, to see that the people of this province are covered in this field and in this area, regardless of any technical detail of where jurisdiction lies.

This is the point. Are they going to exercise their jurisdiction under the British North America Act or are they not? That is the question.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, that is the question. Is this parliament going to exercise its jurisdiction under the British North America Act or is it not? In my submission the future health and development of our banking and commercial institutions is directly dependent upon this parliament occupying fully and occupying now its constitutional jurisdiction.
Where the government has gone wrong in this matter has been, in my view, in its virtual pigeonholing of the whole report of the Porter royal commission. In my view that report is one of the most distinguished state papers ever produced in Canada. It is original and provocative; it blazes new trails while upholding tried concepts. It is a cohesive, packaged document, each part of which is dependent upon the other for its purposeful rationale.
If the government had adopted the recommendations of the Porter commission, had acted boldly and wisely to bring the so-called near banks under the jurisdiction of this parliament, we would not have had this halfhearted, faltering bill before us today. We would have had the package deal which was contemplated by the Porter royal commission, a realistic, cohesive and workable charter for Canada's financial institutions in the ensuing ten years. Instead, in the Bank Act and in this allegedly complementary legislation
Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. which is to create the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, we have a hodgepodge of political compromise, a medley of economic expediency and political contrivance.
Even at this late date I want to plead this afternoon with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) to change his course and to ask parliament to occupy to the limit the federal jurisdiction in banking, financial and commercial matters. It is because I feel so keenly and so deeply that such a course is imperative at this stage of our development in Canada's centennial year that I propose to discuss with some precision, based upon judicial and other authorities, the constitutional problems involved.
In the second edition of his authoritative and scholarly work "Canadian Constitutional Law", Mr. Justice Laskin has this to say at page 590 about the jurisdiction of this parliament:
The B.N.A. Act contains overwhelming internal evidence of the conviction that money, banking and credit (in its public aspect) should be exclusively of federal concern. Among the enumerated classes of subjects in section 91 are (1), currency and coinage (head 14); (2) banking, incorporation of banks and issue of paper money (head 15); (3) savings banks (head 16); (4) bills of exchange and promissory notes (head 18); (5) interest (head 19); and (6) legal tender (head 20): these are in addition to federal power in relation to bankruptcy and insolvency (head 21). From the outset the courts took a broad view of the federal banking power. In Tennant v. Union Bank of Canada (1894) A.C. 31, the Privy Council declared that "banking" was "wide enough to embrace every transaction coming within the legitimate business of a banker"; and see also Merchants Bank v. Smith (1884) 8 S.C.R. 512. Its opinion did not vary over the years as is indicated in Reference re Alberta Bill of Rights Act, A.G. Alta v. A.G. Canada (1947) A.C. 503, where it reaffirmed a consistent course of decision that what is fairly included within the conception of "banking" is a matter reserved exclusively for parliament and this without any limitation to the extent and kind of business that was carried on by banks in Canada in 1867.
The basic issue is, what is "banking"? I have reviewed all the authorities in the courts, in the texts and in so far as I could find them in state papers and I propose to make reference to a number of these authorities. Without hesitation I submit, indeed I assert, that all authorities, with the exception of one court of first instance in British Columbia and one basically irrelevant decision in the Manitoba Court of Appeal, have given to the word "banking" the widest connotation, certainly wide enough to bring in the near banks and wide enough to make the legislation which is before us compulsory and imperative. I put it to the minister, does he
February 3, 1967

Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. think for a moment the learned and distinguished Chief Justice of Ontario, a man with such experience both in the political and legal fields as well as the constitutional field, made his recommendation that near banks should be brought under federal jurisdiction without thought of the constitutional problem?
[DOT] (2.40 p.m.)
Sir, the most recent and authoritative discussion on the word "banking" was in the English Court of Appeal before a very strong court consisting of the Master of the Rolls, Lord Denning, and Lords Justices Harman and Diplock, in the case of United Dominion Trust v. Kirkwood, reported in 1966-you see this is up to date, Mr. Speaker-All England Reports at page 968. The issue there was whether United Dominion Trust was a money lender or a banker, and at page 974 Lord Denning pointed out that the parliament of Westminster-indeed like this parliament-had never defined the word "bank". He said:
So one sees that parliament has conferred many privileges on "banks" and "bankers", but it has never defined what is a "bank" and who is a "banker". It has said many times that a banker is a person who carries on "the business of banking", but it has never told us what is the business of banking. It has imposed penalties on persons who describe themselves as a "bank" or "bankers" when they are not, but it has never told us how to decide whether or not they are bankers.
Lord Denning himself undertook to try to do that and at page 975, after considering all tire earlier authorities, which incidentally are collected immediately after the headnote of the case and are very helpful to any student in this field, Lord Denning went on to say:
There are, therefore, two characteristics usually found in bankers today: (i) they accept money from, and collect cheques for, their customers and place them to their credit; (ii) they honour cheques or orders drawn on them by their customers when presented for payment and debit their customers accordingly. These two characteristics carry with them also a third, namely, (iii) they keep current accounts, or something of that nature, in their books in which the credits and debits are entered.
These characteristics, I submit, Mr. Speaker, are exactly the characteristics of the deposit-taking business conducted by all the so-called near banks in Canada, however, these near banks may in fact be incorporated.
Lord Justice Diplock added these remarks which are to be found at page 986 of the report, and while I apologize for quoting at such length, I believe these statements are of sufficient significance to be put on the record:
What I think is common to all modern definitions and essential to the carrying on of the business of

banking is that the banker should accept from his customers loans of money on "deposit", that is to say, loans for an indefinite period on running account, repayable as to the whole or any part thereof on demand by the customer either without notice or on an agreed period of notice. Some verbal confusion and perhaps some misunderstanding of the less recent judgments may arise from the fact that an account kept by a banker of his customer's loans made without interest and repayable on demand, is nowadays generally called a "current account", while the account kept of his customer's loans made at interest and repayable only on notice is generally known as a "deposit account". Accounts of both these types, however, possess the essential characteristics of running accounts of "deposits" of money by the customer.
Accordingly it is, in my view, essential to the business of banking that a banker should accept money from his customers on a running account into which sums of money are from time to time paid by the customer and from time to time withdrawn by him by cheque, draft or order. I am inclined to agree with Lord Denning, M.R., and the author of the current edition of Paget on Banking (6th Edn.) that to constitute the business of banking today the banker must also undertake to pay cheques drawn on himself (the banker) by his customers in favour of third parties up to the amount standing to their credit in their "current accounts" and to collect cheques for his customers and credit the proceeds to their current accounts. This view of the essential characteristics of the business of banking today is supported by the evidence of the witnesses who were unquestionably bankers who gave expert evidence in the present case.
That long definition of banking is one which I believe our Supreme Court, which pays the very highest respect to the English Court of Appeal, on this basis could not fail to hold that near banks in their deposit business are carrying on the business of banking, the regulation of which under section 91 belongs exclusively to this parliament.
I point out to the minister that Canadian governments in the past have not been so fearful and reluctant as the minister now is to assert federal authority. In 1906 the then minister of justice, Sir Allan Aylesworth, took specific exception to a Quebec act amending the charter of Imperial Trust Company authorizing that company to receive money on deposit and allow interest, and to purchase bills of exchange. In his report to cabinet Sir Allan said:
The undersigned does not admit that these powers may be conferred by the legislature.
Similar objections were raised by Sir Allan Aylesworth in 1910 to a Quebec act incorporating The General Trust, and in a report of January 12, 1911 he expressed the opinion that the powers "infringed upon the subject of banking under any fair interpretation of the word". I emphasize Sir Allan's statement "under any fair interpretation of the word".

Since the provincial government of that day in Quebec refused to amend the act, Sir Allan in a further report dated May 23, 1911 recommended disallowance. At that time he said this, and I think this is a statement of some significance:
The nature of the business of banking is part of the law merchant, and is judicially noticed. If from this business, as so recognized, be excluded the authority to receive money on deposit, to lend money to individuals, except upon the security of bills of exchange, and generally to do an exchange business, the undersigned-
That is Sir Allan.
-apprehends that the peculiar business of banking would not only be affected, but very considerably diminished. The expression "banking" as used in section 91 of the British North America Act, 1867, is, in the opinion of the undersigned, intended to describe not only such powers as are inherently banking powers, but, also, those which were, under the laws of the provinces at the time of the Union, exercised by the banks in the carrying on of their business, and it includes everything within legitimate banking business as it is practised, or has been developed. It may be seen by reference to pre-Union legislation that the deposit of money at interest, and dealing in exchange were expressly authorized banking transactions in the province. Leading decisions in the United States, also, show that such powers are attributed to the banks in that country. In fact it seems impossible to suppose that these powers are not necessarily common to all well-ordered banking systems.
This opinion of an earlier minister of justice is, I think, of real significance and I wish that the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Cardin) would take as strong a position in advising the Minister of Finance.

I point out to the minister that the question of whether Montreal Trust Company was a banking institution within the meaning of that term in an agreement to subscribe for shares that "this underwriting may be pledged or hypothecated with any banking institution" was discussed in Montreal Trust Company v. Richardson, (1921) 62 S.C.R. 617. The trial judge, Mr. Justice Rose, who subsequently became a great and distinguished chief justice of the Supreme Court of Ontario, and on appeal the Chief Justice of Canada, Sir Louis H. Davies, a former minister of justice, held that the trust company was a "banking institution" within the meaning of that agreement.
Further, sir, I think that the 1938 and 1947 decisions of the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in the references regarding the various Alberta statutes indicate how wide is the federal jurisdiction under banking. In 1947 the Judicial Committee declared a statute of Quebec ultra vires which would have forfeited to the Crown in the right of the province as bona vacantia, deposits in "credit institutions and all other establishments which receive funds or securities on deposits," upon which no claim had been made for 30 years. The case is Attorney General for Canada v. Attorney General for Quebec, (1947) A.C. 33.
The reasons given by Lord Porter make it clear that the deposit contract is the heart of banking. The argument of counsel for the Attorney General of Canada, Mr. H. E. O'Donnell, K.C., a distinguished counsel and son in law of Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, and W. R. Jackett, now the distinguished President of the Exchequer Court is, I think, most interesting. On page 35 I note this sentence from their argument:
The Quebec statute strikes at the very heart and core of banking as used in section 91-the deposit contract and the rights and obligations flowing therefrom being a most essential part of banking.

Canada Deposit Insurance Corp.
There, in one sentence, is the pith and substance of my argument. The heart and core of banking is the deposit contract. That is why I assert that these deposit-taking institutions are under federal jurisdiction, and we in this parliament should assert our authority without equivocating.
Earlier in my remarks I said that there are two troublesome Canadian	cases-troublesome to my argument. I believe in mentioning anything that is troublesome. The first case is in re Dominion Trust Company and United States Fidelity Claim, (1918) 3 W.W.R. 1023. The headnote reads:
A provincial legislature has power to incorporate a company with the object of carrying on that branch of banking which consists of accepting money on deposits, paying interest thereon and allowing the customer to issue cheques against such deposit.
Personally I deny that and I submit that the parliament of Canada can intervene to stop this practice. This was a case before a single judge, Mr. Justice Murphy at trial, and the issue was never presented as to what would happen if parliament fully occupied the field. It is clear that grave injustice would have resulted in this case if Mr. Justice Murphy had held otherwise. The old maxim "hard cases make bad law" is especially applicable. In any event it is clear that Murphy J. had grave doubts about his decision because he said:
In the absence of authority, I decline as a judge of first instance, to place a construction on that statute which would have disastrous results on the business of numerous provincial companies.
The other case is in the Manitoba Court of Appeal, re Bergethaler Waiseman-a corporation apparently from the constituency of the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson). The case is reported in (1948) 1 D.L.R. 761.
The company was incorporated by special act of the Manitoba legislature, with the usual powers of a trust company. For some 23 years it carried on business in the Mennonite community (1) as an administrator of estates and (2) as a deposit business, that is, receiving money on deposit, repayable on demand, and dealing with the money as its own. It went into liquidation and it was claimed that the actions of the company were ultra vires its powers under provincial legislation.
I point out that in this case, there are clear distinctions, of which two are most important. First, in this institution in Manitoba, no cheques could be drawn by customers on their own account; second, withdrawals were not in cash but by cheques issued by the

company to its customers drawn upon a chartered bank. It was held that this company was not in the banking business, and I personally believe it was not. It is clear that it was not carrying on a true deposit business. This case has been referred to me on different occasions as the authority for the reluctance of the minister. I submit that it is no authority at all. I submit that neither of these cases is in any way an authority for weakening the exclusive legislative authority of this parliament over the business of banking coming within the normal and natural meaning of that word. I submit that meaning is clear and unequivocal and includes the deposit business of the near banks.
Sir, it may probably be said that I am making a lawyer's case this afternoon; perhaps I am, and I do not apologize for that. Perhaps that is needed from time to time in this chamber. In other days men trained at the bar were prepared to argue legal and constitutional issues in this chamber, and personally I believe we slough off such problems much too readily upon the vague and undetermined group yclept "the law officers of the crown".
I return to my original submission, and I advance it in all earnestness to the Minister of Finance, that the business of the near banks is banking within the meaning of section 91 of the British North America Act and as a result all such deposit business should be brought under the control of parliament.
I have shown that the Premier and the Minister of Financial and Commercial Affairs of Ontario apparently agree with my argument this afternoon. I say that this legislation should be made universal and compulsory for all institutions accepting deposits from the public. Unless it is, I submit this bill is defective and indeed may be mischievous. The legislation may result in a hodgepodge of deposit-taking institutions, with fantastic, dangerous variations across the country. There may be insured institutions in Ottawa and non-insured institutions in Hull, insured institutions in Sackville and non-insured institutions in Amherst. The provincial boundaries, I hope, are invisible in this country. In my opinion such a hodgepodge inevitably would lead to confusion. It might be mischievous and dangerous.
I say to the Minister of Finance this afternoon that there is still time for boldness and for wisdom on his part. Let him move in and occupy the full jurisdiction of this parliament. If he fails to do so he will cause irreparable harm to our financial institutions which have

been, traditionally, among the soundest and most progressive in the world. Their integrity, their future development, are imperative to our national development. Let not the hon. member for Eglinton fail them today.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first thank the house for the way in which it has proceeded to debate this bill and to give it careful but not too prolonged attention. I am grateful for this because I believe it is important to proceed with this legislation as soon as possible.
First, may I comment on the remarks made by my learned friend the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell) who gave us a most interesting and erudite discourse on the meaning of banking within the British North America Act. I hope his view of the ambit of the banking clause is justified. As he admitted, however, there are some doubts. There are some learned people who even disagree with my learned friend from Carleton. Perhaps if he had spoken first they would not have had the temerity to do so. At any rate he does agree there are some who do not share his views or the views of the other authorities he quoted.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
I am inclined to agree with him that the powers of parliament over banking are very extensive. Why then have I hesitated so far to proceed with legislation? I have felt that even though it might have been possible to go further in extending our legislative jurisdiction over banking it was important, first of all, to deal with urgent problems, and one of the urgent problems is the insurance of deposits, something upon which there has been widespread agreement in the house. I believe it is important, at this stage of the development of our financial institutions, that the ordinary citizen, who is not in much of a position to tell the difference between the financial worth of the institutions that are competing for his deposits, should have some assurance that his savings are not going to be

destroyed by depositing them with an institution that founders either because of lack of liquidity or because of bad management.
If we had proceeded otherwise, if we had proceeded on the assumption that our legislation extending jurisdiction in the field of banking would be valid, we would nevertheless risk the possibility that, notwithstanding the confidence which we might have in all the authorities, including the hon. member for Carleton (Mr. Bell), about the scope of federal jurisdiction, someone would have the temerity to challenge it, in which case there would have been long delays while our legislation was being tested in the courts before it could become effective. Therefore I felt it was important that we should proceed along lines that I believed would not arouse such a challenge.
Moreover this is the reason why, in the legislation that is before us, we are requiring that the provinces should agree before any provincial institution accepts deposit insurance. We do not want to risk the possibility of a challenge which would interfere with the extension of deposit insurance as quickly as possible to as many depositors and as many institutions as possible.
From the discussions I have had personally with provincial ministers and that my officials have had with provincial officials, I know that in practically all of the provinces of this country there is a desire that this legislation come into effect immediately. The Attorney General of the province of British Columbia has said that he will recommend that institutions which accept deposits in that province should be compelled to take out federal insurance. I am hopeful that other provinces will do likewise because nothing will serve better to make this system universal throughout the country than declarations like that by various provincial governments.
I say that because a provincial deposit-taking institution may be able to get some insurance for its deposits within the province of its incorporation, but I do not think that any province would have the power to insure deposits taken by its institution in another province. Therefore if the province of British Columbia, for example, were to compel all deposit-taking institutions, whether British Columbian, federal or provincial, to be federally insured, then a trust company incorporated, say, in the province of Quebec would be unable to accept deposits in the province of British Columbia unless it were federally insured. This is the argument for federal jurisdiction in this field.
February 3, 1967	COMMONS
It is important that we should have uniform financial regulations, uniform banking regulations and uniform laws in relation to banking generally. I do not dispute this point at all. However, Mr. Speaker, I do suggest to the house that this is the practical thing to do under existing circumstances in order to extend the kind of protection and inspection that is so much needed across the country.
There are one or two other points upon which I should comment. First, I should add a word or two to what I said in my opening speech with respect to the interim arrangements. I have made two proposals, one of which is in the bill and the other in my speech. In the bill it is provided that provincial institutions may be insured with the approval of the provincial authorities, the provincial governments.
I also said in my opening speech today that in order to expedite the extension of insurance to provincial institutions it was contemplated that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation would be prepared to cover all the deposit-accepting trust and loan companies of a province if the province concerned so requests even before the corporation has made an examination into the affairs of the individual companies and ascertained if they are eligible to pay for insurance.
I went on say that the provinces will be expected to accept some share of financial responsibility during the period while these institutions have not been examined to see whether they comply with the requirements of the corporation itself. I think this is a proper step to take because I feel it is most important the scheme should come into effect as soon as possible and that it should come into effect uniformly.
I do not believe it would be adequate to bring institutions in as we find the time and the men to do the inspections. I believe we will have to take some chances and bring in the provincial institutions even before there has been adequate time for this work. If a province agrees to this and makes some arrangements about sharing the financial costs or losses, then we can accomplish our major objective.
Some question was raised about the definition of deposits. It is a very technical question. I hope we can defer it until we get the bill before the committee on finance, to which I intend to refer it after second reading.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) asked me who will receive the dividends of the corporation. The answer is that I
Canada Deposit Insurance Corp. will as Minister of Finance. These accrue only to the federal government; there are no other shareholders of the corporation.
The hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton) asked if I would consider the possibility of a differential in premiums because of the difference in risks. We gave some consideration to that possibility but we discarded it because, even though we are confident our federal institutions are sound and are adequately supervised, there may be other provincial institutions that are equally sound, and the problem of trying to differentiate between the financial integrity of institutions would be beyond the capacity of the corporation. Therefore we have decided that it would be better to have a uniform premium.
I thought that in the course of his remarks the hon. member for Kamloops suggested that the only pressures were coming from the, shall I say, less viable institutions, from those institutions whose standards are not as high as the banks and federal trust and loan companies. This is not altogether true. Perhaps the best example is what happened the other day with the Montreal City and District Bank, which is probably one of the soundest and most conservatively managed banks in the country, and yet there was a run on it. That run was based on ignorance but these things can happen in the best regulated institutions. The existence of deposit insurance would have prevented that run. The depositors would have known that their money was safe. This is an argument altogether apart from the question of improving the financial standards of institutions for deposit insurance on a universal basis.
I think that is enough for me to say at this time, Mr. Speaker. When the bill is before the standing committee on finance I shall have a few minor amendments to propose to it.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a few remarks on clause 2 of the bill. In
Development of Film Industry doing so, at the outset I would say that I thoroughly agree with the motives of the minister and of this legislation in attempting to set up a truly Canadian feature film industry. As I look at clause 2 I can see its many advantages to film-makers in this country. It will give an opportunity to our creative artists, writers, producers, technicians, and what have you, to produce feature films.
Over the past few months on the few occasions this matter has been before the house in resolution and bill form many eloquent speeches have been made. I have no desire to be repetitious in this regard, but would point out that while Canada would rate only a footnote, I suppose, in any book on the world's best motion pictures, films have been made in this country since before 1900. That is a long time ago. So we already have a good basis in this country on which to build a feature film industry.
It may be of interest to hon. members to know that from 1917 to 1930 feature motion films were made in Canada. They were filmed in Ottawa, Montreal, Trenton, Cobourg, Toronto, Calgary, Fort William, Saint John, Banff, Vancouver and Victoria-in fact, all across the country. These were not shorts and productions of that nature, they were feature films. Admittedly, many of them were failures and did not make much money but some of them did make money. It is an interesting sidelight to note that the most expensive and ambitious of these was a film called "Carry on Sergeant", filmed in Trenton, Ontario. It cost $500,000, which was at that time, and is still, a considerable amount of money. At that time it was a very large sum indeed. Unfortunately in the United States, at exactly the time this silent film was to be distributed, a film called "The Jazz Singer", starring A1 Jolson, appeared and opened the era of talking pictures. That was, of course, the first talking motion picture. As a result the Canadian production "Carry on Sergeant" was not able to carry on at all and fell flat on its financial face.
We are all aware of the success of the National Film Board, Crawley Films and other private companies. I will not go into that matter further. So we do have an honoured tradition in film making in this country. It is possible, and I emphasize the word "possible", to make Canadian films with Canadian people involved. It will probably come as a surprise to the minister to realize that in my home constituency of Saskatoon, the garden city of the prairies, if I may speak with pardonable pride, even there in the vast expanses of
February 3, 1967

Development of Film Industry western Canada we have a budding film industry. We have there, under the very capable direction of Mr. Richard Savage, a theatrical company known as the Circle in the Centre. Incidentally, it is a professional theatrical company and is in better financial condition than any other such company in Canada, including the Neptune in Halifax and certainly the Crest in Toronto. Our professional theatrical company is in the black and has already produced one talking picture. Admittedly it is only half an hour in length, but nevertheless it is of excellent quality. This is a beginning of what can be achieved in this part of the world. This illustrates the fact that we have a very useful motion picture industry in western Canada.
I should now like to return to my earlier statement that it is possible to make Canadian films with Canadian personnel involved. I say it is possible, but is it probable? If we pass this bill, as I am sure we shall, will we be providing loans or backing for Canadian filmmakers, producers, technicians and what have you? Frankly, Mr. Chairman, in the present situation I do not believe this is probable. What we will be doing is providing money to film-makers and technicians in Canada, but the choice of who is to be involved in these productions will be strictly under the control of a union in the United States of America.
Clause 2 of the bill defines film activity, film-maker, film production and film technician. When one considers this matter one finds that these people are controlled from New York. Are we going to give money collected through taxes on our people to a Canadian film industry and then have no say or have our say interfered with by an international union with regard to who shall be involved in production? This is a problem about which I am sure the minister is more than aware. I have grave doubts about voting for a bill that will provide money for a Canadian film industry which, as I have said, will actually be controlled from New York, Chicago or Hollywood.
Until that matter is settled this bill will be just another example of subsidizing the United States by tax dollars from Canadian citizens, and I think this is deplorable. Anything which militates against Canadian sovereignty I must in all conscience oppose. I see the minister is nodding her head. I know she knows the union to which I am referring, the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees and Moving Picture Machine Operators of the United States and Canada,


known shortly as IATSE. When you listen to the word IATSE you realize it has a certain connotation which will be obvious in a moment.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
As I have mentioned, its headquarters are in New York, Chicago and Hollywood. Admittedly the union of electricians and stage hands based in Toronto does have some Canadian autonomy and is able to make some decisions based on Canadian problems. However, I would defy anyone to produce a film without cameramen. It is very difficult indeed. Local 644 in Toronto is merely a branch. The headquarters of this union are in New York and all the executive officers reside there. Its interests are United States interests, not Canadian. For example, the contract which the producers of a film in this country sign must be dictated by New York. This is certainly true in the eastern part of Canada. I believe it is true that one of the sections of the contract states that there shall be no use of British cameramen or other technical personnel in the production of a film unless specifically agreed to by the New York headquarters. Of course in most instances they will not agree. In other words they say: Do as we say or we will throw a picket line around you and put you out of business. This is what has happened.
I have before me a brief presented by the Canadian film cameramen's local to IATSE. I should like to read into the record part of what the Canadian film cameramen say about this problem. It appears on page 3 of the brief which was presented in 1964. May I say to the house once again that the problems I am delineating today will be brought before the executive officers of IATSE this evening in Toronto. The brief reads in part as follows:
Canadian cameramen are getting no professional recognition because when a producer wishes to use a union crew in Canada he must contact the New York or Hollywood local and these locals would give preference to their own American members. In fact, they have done little for the film cameramen employed in Canada, and as far as that goes, in the Canadian film industry generally. It is understandably so if you consider that their own organizers and business agents are concerned mainly with the affairs in the United States which are vastly greater than the problems in Canada.
Then the brief goes on to describe the problem which they had in Toronto with a local business agent from New York who came to Canada and created such a terrible impression that they got together and threw him out.

At the top of page 4 the brief goes on to say:
Moreover, the interest of the United States locals 644 and 659 are diametrically opposed to the interest of their Canadian members. To the American cameramen's locals, films for T.V. and features made anywhere outside of New York or Hollywood are second rate, and an encroachment of their security and they would be quite happy to see Canada without any film industry whatever.
What a formidable obstacle to place before the best intentioned bill of the minister which we are discussing now. With such an obstacle it will be very difficult to establish a truly Canadian feature film industry. Unfortunately, as the minister knows only too well, the problem is still before us even as we discuss this bill. This group has asked, and is asking again tonight, that local 644 allow the Canadian cameramen to form an autonomous Canadian union so that Canadian problems can be decided here and not in New York. The brief continues:
Moreover, we feel that if the charter was granted to those in Canada that the International would, in fact, make a real contribution to the development of the Canadian film industry.
It can be asked: why do they not join another union or form their own? As the minister knows, it has been tried. They have not been able to get local autonomy. They went to Claude Jodoin of the Canadian Labour Congress but he refused to interfere. He said it was a local problem. After all, we must recognize that the C.L.C. is also affiliated with some United States unions. Perhaps this is understandable. Some employees of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and of the National Film Board have formed a local union with the C.N.T.U. However, I will not go into details on that. The whole matter is in a state of flux right now. In looking at this bill one might say that it is a wonderful idea to have film-makers, film technicians and film producers creating Canadian films. Yet this will not actually happen until something is done to overcome the problem of United States domination of the Canadian film industry. Our Canadian sovereignty is a matter of paramount importance which must be settled before this bill goes into effect. I would certainly like to hear the minister's view on how she intends to do this before money is allotted to Canadian film-makers.
In Saturday Night of September, 1966 there was an excellent article describing the situation. The headline reads: "Thanks, Yanks, For All That You've Done, or Why There Isn't A Canadian Feature Film Industry". The article is written by Harold Arthur. The subheading
Development of Film Industry reads: "Unless A big American Union Called IATSE Is Forced To Re-assess Its Role, The Industry Is Doomed". I have spoken to film cameramen in this country, as I know the minister has, and they agree with this assessment.
Of course the matter of distribution is very important. The minister knows only too well that every feature film that is produced must be 99.441 per cent IATSE-like the soap-and must have a IATSE seal before the distributors will touch it. What can this union do if we do not go along with them? As is stated on page 1 of this article:
In effect, what IATSE demands is that Canadians should play by American rules, but with none of the Americans' advantages.. .In other words, as far as IATSE is concerned, we are not supposed to make features at all.
Farther down it reads:
Whether they admit it or not, IATSE in Canada owe first allegiance to headquarters in the U.S.A.
There is one pungent comment here regarding what some of the members of the local would not do without first getting permission from the United States, but in the interests of parliamentary usage I will refrain from quoting that portion of the article. However, I would like to read an example of what a big United States union can do to a Canadian production. The article reads as follows:
As an example of what the cameramen can do when they have the help of the 873 members-
That is local 873, composed of electricians, etc.
-there was the incident last summer when a crew from Labrinthe (the National Flm Board's contribution to Expo) arrived in Toronto to film a circus sequence at Maple Leaf Gardens. Telling the story, Cole, the Toronto business agent-
I understand the minister knows him very well.
-comes on as the unhyphenated Canadian. "This was supposed to be a Canadian project for all the world to see," he says, "and we thought they should have a Canadian cameraman". What happened was that IATSE objected to the presence of Walter Lassaly, internationally renowned British cameraman (Tom Jones, Zorba the Greek), who had been hired by the Film Board specially for the project. "We have Canadians right here who could have done the job as well," said Cole, "so we threw them (the National Film Board) out of the Gardens. I'd do it again if I had to."
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Since Cole had the support of IATSE electricians at the Gardens there was nothing the Labrinthe people could do. Had they tried to start filming, IATSE could have pulled the switch and put Gardens, circus, and spectators in darkness. The Film Board retreated.

The author of the article goes on to wonder if they would have objected as strongly if Lassaly had been from the United States. I continue the quotation:
To Canadian film workers, that's a wonderful straight line. What puts a final, baffling seal to it all is that the circus sequence was eventually filmed successfully in Milwaukee, in the good old U.S. of A.
This is a classic example of what can be done. You may perhaps wonder, Mr. Chairman, why with the tremendous power this union exerts on Canadian cameramen they would want to join that union or have a local here. Why would they not be happier with their own organization in this country, because the distributors undoubtedly would distribute film as long as there was a union label on it? I think the answer is an honest one, and it comes from these cameramen. They need the help and the experience of the cameramen and others in the IATSE organization in the United States. They need their help. If they get an autonomous local here, they need to be able to go back and forth and ask for help. They need to have this type of experienced help in order to build up a reasonable film industry.
In addition they need the right, and it is in the bill, if they want to make a contract with British film-makers to be able to do so without IATSE excluding the British film-makers. I think this is a serious problem of Canadian autonomy and it relates to what we are going to do with the $10 million and whether it is going to be controlled from the good old United States.
I am sorry the Minister of Manpower and Immigration is not in the house because with his vast experience with unions he could perhaps shed some light on what could be done about urging the union, with its headquarters in New York, to allow an autonomous union here. Perhaps something could be done through the Department of External Affairs with the Secretary of State of the United States to urge upon the union the necessity for allowing a totally autonomous Canadian branch. I feel this is a very difficult question with which to deal. I should like to hear what the minister has to say on this important question. I, of course, support the principle of the bill the minister has introduced because I believe in the idea. I believe it is a marvellous idea. However, I feel we must be able to make these films without any United States strings attached. fMr. Brand.]

Mr. Chairman, I have not discussed this particular point with the officials who were advising us in the drafting of this legislation, but I think that the purpose of the presence of the film commissioner is a fairly clear-cut one.
As the hon. member probably knows, countries may sign cultural agreements. Canada has already signed a cultural agreement with the Republic of France. Such an agreement has been under negotiation for some time with the United Kingdom and with Italy; and I discussed this with the appropriate minister and officials while I was in Italy in the fall.
The signing of such agreements will also permit the signing of co-production agreements between countries. Once those agreements are in force the individual agreements between individual companies may be made. The co-production agreements are, we feel, particularly important because again they are the key to distribution abroad, particularly in countries like Italy where the actual movie houses themselves are owned or influenced by the state. Such agreements can guarantee that Canadian movies at once have entree to all of the hundreds and hundreds of movie houses throughout Italy.
So the film commissioner, Mr. Chairman, as the managing head of the film board is the person responsible for advising my office and the government generally on co-production agreements and cultural agreements which may involve film work. Fie is the adviser to the government apropos of films, and it was thought most appropriate that he be there.
However, there is no suggestion-though I think from time to time this may have been raised-that the film board would attempt to strangle this industry to preserve itself. Indeed we think that what may very well happen is that some of the film makers on the film board themselves may, in a sort of moonlighting or part time way, go out and make

their own films and apply for a grant or a loan of one kind or another.
We hope that the two corporations will provide two different slices of the needed pie to produce films for various purposes within and without the country. I really cannot suggest any reason for thinking that there will be any kind of conflict or that the commissioner would have a weighted position on the board. He will simply be there to liaise-and liaison is very important-in the matter of information and expertise between the film board and this new board with respect to eventual agreement.

If I may, Mr. Chairman, this is the very thing I was afraid of, and the minister has spelled it out very clearly.
